name: Note
text: Who is this character, what's their role in the story/game, and what's the ONE thing a viewer should understand about them in under 2 seconds of screen time? Every design decision below should trace back to this line.

name: Note
text: Design in solid black shapes FIRST, no interior detail. A strong character reads correctly as a pure silhouette alone — if two characters look the same as flat shapes, they'll be confused at a glance in motion, no matter how detailed the final art is.

name: Note
text: Real people, actors, or animals whose posture/movement/expression capture this character's personality. A slouched posture, a confident stride, a nervous fidget — reference the SPECIFIC physical trait, not just "this person looks cool."

name: Note
text: A locked palette (2-3 dominant colors, 1 accent) with exact hex values once finalized. Keep it consistent across every piece of concept art for this character — a shifting palette between drawings is the most common character-design inconsistency.

name: Note
text: Outfit variants, key props, and what each one communicates about the character (status, profession, backstory). Note which props are purely decorative vs. functionally important to the story or gameplay.

name: Note
text: The 6-8 expressions this character will actually need on screen (not a generic emotion-wheel dump) — pulled from the actual script or gameplay barks, so nothing critical gets discovered missing mid-production.

name: Note
text: Front, 3/4, side, and back views at a consistent scale, with proportions locked (head-to-body ratio, limb length). This is the reference sheet a rigger, 3D modeler, or another 2D animator builds from — ambiguity here becomes an inconsistency in every downstream department.

name: Note
text: Drop silhouette studies, photo reference for anatomy/costume, and the final turnaround sheet (image cards, or a real 3D model card once the character is blocked out) here — this is what a rigger or 3D artist actually opens first.
